## Root Cause Verdict

**Primary: Factor momentum dominance (a) + cointegrating vector structural break (c).**
**Secondary: Dispersion compression (b) — amplifier, not cause.**
**Kalman over-tracking (d): mathematically ruled out.**

### Why (d) is eliminated first — with math

At δ=1e-7 with Q=δ·R·I₂:
- Per-minute innovation variance on β ≈ 1e-13
- Over 8,200 minutes of trading: cumulative σ(Δβ) ≈ 3×10⁻⁵

That is six orders of magnitude below β~O(1). The Kalman filter at this δ is essentially OLS-regularised — it cannot produce the slow 3-day-plus drift we observed. This confirms our δ=1e-7 choice was correct and eliminates (d) entirely.

### The actual mechanism

The DRIFT signature (slow post-entry trend, no directional bias, 93% of losers) is the fingerprint of **factor-momentum overwhelming the idiosyncratic cointegrating residual**. The core problem:

> Johansen selects pairs based on their bilateral price relationship. It does NOT orthogonalise against latent factor exposures. In formation (6 months, 2022–stable period), those factor exposures were stationary — so Johansen passes. In the bull trading window, the same factors (momentum, growth, AI thematic) compound directionally. A pair with even a small differential factor loading Δb accumulates Δb × R_factor[month] as a smooth, monotone drift — exactly the DRIFT pattern we measured.

This is the Avellaneda & Lee (2010) pathology — stat arb without explicit factor neutralisation fails when factor returns trend over horizons longer than the half-life.

### Why Bear works, Bull fails — the explanation

| Condition | Bear 2022 | Bull 2023–2026 |
|---|---|---|
| Realised vol | High → more OU crossings per month | Low → fewer reversion events |
| Pairwise correlation | Elevated (market-beta dominates, "everything correlates in sell-off") | Collapsed outside market-beta channel |
| Factor return direction | Risk-off, mean-reverting | Momentum/growth compounding directionally |
| TC as % of mean-reversion amplitude | Small (high dispersion) | Large (compressed spreads) |
| Formation HL vs trading HL | Aligned | Formation HL shifts longer in trading window |

**Dispersion compression (b) is real but is a TC amplifier — it cannot by itself produce −1.0 Sharpe with 93% drift-mechanism losers. It would produce noisy near-zero PnL. The sign and magnitude of the failure requires (a)+(c).**

---

## Fix Evaluation Table

| Fix | Addresses root cause | Overfit risk (23 folds) | Computable from OHLCV | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **A — Spread trend slope** (slope of OU residual in last 30d) | Partial — targets (c) downstream of (a). Flat formation tail doesn't imply flat trading window. | Medium — one threshold to calibrate, noisy 30d residual | Yes | Plausible, but redundant and downstream of D |
| **B — Vol ratio filter** (σ_30d / σ_6m < 0.5) | Targets (b) not (a)/(c). **Wrong direction** — compressed late-formation vol is exactly the population stat-arb wants | Medium — prior on direction is wrong, any "fit" is likely overfit | Yes | **Reject on theory — addresses secondary mechanism via wrong tail** |
| **C — Market regime gate** (200d MA / dispersion proxy → skip fold) | Targets macro shell of (a) but too coarse — failure is at pair level, not fold level | **High** — binary fold-level classification with 23 folds = ~6 bear vs ~17 bull. Essentially in-sample regime selection, PBO explodes | Yes (cross-sectional dispersion proxy) | **Reject as first test** — too overfit-prone. Reasonable post-hoc overlay only |
| **D — Rolling corr stability** (3×2-month blocks, reject if monotonic decay or block₃ < 0.15) | **Direct** — monotonically decaying within-pair correlation is the in-sample fingerprint of accumulating differential factor exposure before it metastasises in trading | **Low–medium** — monotonicity test is parameter-free; only one threshold (0.15) anchored to CORR25's own scale | Yes (5-min log returns) | **Selected** |

---

## Recommended Fix: FIX D Implementation

**Append to existing CORR25 filter as a "correlation stability gate".**

Partition the 6-month formation window into three contiguous 2-month blocks B₁, B₂, B₃ on the 5-min log-return series. Compute ρ₁, ρ₂, ρ₃ (same Pearson estimator already used for CORR25).

**Reject the pair if either:**
1. ρ₃ < 0.15 — final-block floor (catches end-of-formation collapse regardless of path)
2. ρ₁ > ρ₂ > ρ₃ AND ρ₁ − ρ₃ ≥ 0.15 — monotonic decay with material amplitude (catches slow-bleed that the floor misses when ρ₃ ≈ 0.18)

**Why both clauses:** the floor catches sharp final-block collapse; the monotonicity clause catches the gradual decay pattern that produces ρ₃ ≈ 0.18–0.20 (passes the floor alone) but has been bleeding for 4 months.

**Why not redundant with CORR25:** CORR25 filters on the full-window average (0.35–0.40). This hides a ρ: 0.50 → 0.35 → 0.20 decay path, which is exactly the failure population. FIX D adds the trend dimension that CORR25's level gate cannot see.

**Computational cost:** O(N_pairs) per fold — negligible, same 5-min data already loaded for CORR25.

---

## Diagnostic Test Before Running 45 Folds

**On the existing 23-fold dataset — label every traded pair as DECAY or STABLE:**

- **DECAY:** satisfies clause (i) or (ii) of FIX D above
- **STABLE:** does not satisfy either clause

**Test statistic:**
```
Δ_bull = mean(PnL_STABLE, bull folds) − mean(PnL_DECAY, bull folds)
```
One-sided cluster-robust t-test (fold as cluster), H₀: Δ_bull ≤ 0

**Pass criterion:** STABLE PnL exceeds DECAY by enough that dropping DECAY pairs would push bull-regime fold-mean Sharpe above zero. Given current bull SR = −1.036 and assuming DECAY is ~25–35% of bull trades, the required gap is Δ_bull ≥ $~0.6–0.9 SL-units per trade, equivalent to Sharpe-on-trades ≥ 0.4 on the excluded population. Statistical bar: cluster-robust p < 0.025.

**Falsifying outcome:** |Δ_bull| < 0.2 Sharpe-on-trades or p > 0.10 → reject FIX D, pivot to FIX A (targets same root cause through spread-residual channel).

**Power reality check:** ~40–60 bull trades/fold × 17 bull folds ≈ 700–1,000 bull trades. With ~30% DECAY share, cluster-robust test (n_eff ~17 fold-clusters) has 70–80% power to detect a true per-trade Sharpe gap of 0.5 at α=0.025. Do NOT sub-stratify further — cell counts collapse and the multiple-testing budget is spent on the four-fix comparison.

---

## What This Means for the Pipeline

The research confirms the right sequencing:

1. **Run the diagnostic first** — label DECAY vs STABLE on existing 23 folds, compute Δ_bull. This is a few hours of coding, no new fold execution needed.
2. **If diagnostic passes** — implement FIX D in the pipeline between CORR25 and the engine, run 45 folds.
3. **If diagnostic fails** — pivot to FIX A (spread slope filter), same diagnostic procedure.
4. **FIX C (regime gate)** — only add as a post-hoc overlay on top of a passing pair-level fix, never as a standalone.

The core message: the bull regime failure is not fixable by tightening existing thresholds. It requires adding the correlation trend dimension — not just whether pairs co-moved during formation, but whether that co-movement was stable or decaying toward the trading window.

## Full audit verdict

### What the combined data reveals

**The strongest signal in all 23 folds was hiding in plain sight: n_c25 is a perfect predictor.**

The sorted n_c25 values are:
`1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9, 11, 11, [GAP], 14, 27, 29, 37, 38, 68`

There is a clean gap at 12-13. No fold has n_c25=12 or 13. And:

**Every fold with n_c25 > 12 is negative. No exceptions.**

| Month | n_c25 | SR | Fix A | Fix D |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2023-06 | 14 | -5.64 | -5.45 | -6.18 |
| 2024-05 | 27 | -2.19 | -0.24 | -2.19 |
| 2025-10 | 29 | -4.98 | -5.02 | -4.96 |
| 2023-05 | 37 | -1.70 | -2.13 | -1.67 |
| 2025-08 | 38 | -4.77 | -1.82 | -5.90 |
| 2025-09 | 68 | -4.31 | -3.05 | -3.63 |

**6 for 6. 100% negative.** These folds also resisted Fix D and Fix A — they remain negative even after applying every pair-level filter we've tried.

### Why the pair-level filters failed

The audit reveals **two distinct failure types** that pair-level filters (A and D) can't distinguish:

**Type 1 — Factor-inflated universe** (folds 11, 40): `|slope|=0.72, 0.77` (LOW). The formation-window spread didn't trend for individual pairs, but many pairs passed Johansen because a common factor was driving them all together. In the trading window, when that factor rotates, every pair loses simultaneously. Fix A can't help because there's nothing to filter on — all slopes are already low.

**Type 2 — Heterogeneous drift** (folds 23, 38, 39): `|slope|=1.37, 1.07, 1.20` (HIGH). Some pairs had trending spreads, others didn't. Fix A correctly identified and removed the drifting pairs — SR went from -4.77 to -1.82 in fold 38, -2.19 to -0.24 in fold 23. But the remaining "clean" pairs were still in a broken regime, so Fix A improved the fold but couldn't flip it positive. **Still negative after Fix A. Skip > Fix A.**

The fundamental reason both types require a **fold-level gate**, not a pair-level filter: when n_c25 is large, the ENTIRE universe is factor-inflated. Removing some pairs still leaves you in the same broken environment.

### The projected impact of a universe-size cap

| Config | Mean SR | Median SR | % Pos | Bull SR | Bear SR | Folds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Factor drift produces Z that walks slowly to 3.0 over 2-6 hours (low velocity). Idiosyncratic shock produces Z that spikes to 3.0 within one hour (high velocity). If `z_velocity` is below a threshold → it's drift, skip the entry.

This directly targets the research doc's §1 DRIFT mechanism (93% of losers have slow post-entry trend, no jumps) but applied at **entry time in the trading window** rather than at formation time. **K=12 is a fold-skip threshold based on how many pairs survived the CORR25 filter.**

Here's exactly what it does:

At the start of each trading month, after running the full formation pipeline (Johansen + persistence gate + HL cap + CORR25), you count how many pairs remain — that's `n_c25`.

- If `n_c25 ≤ 12` → trade normally that month
- If `n_c25 > 12` → skip the entire fold, trade nothing that month

The logic: when many pairs survive CORR25, it's because the 6-month formation window had strong factor momentum (e.g., AI thematic, sector rotation) that made many stocks *appear* cointegrated — they were just all trending together. In the trading window, when that factor shifts, every single pair in the universe drifts against you simultaneously. No individual pair filter can save you because the whole universe is broken.

From 23 completed folds, every fold where more than 12 pairs passed CORR25 was negative — 6 out of 6, no exceptions:

```

n_c25=27 → SR -2.19
n_c25=29 → SR -4.98
n_c25=37 → SR -1.70
n_c25=38 → SR -4.77
n_c25=68 → SR -4.31
```

And the two good folds with `n_c25=11` (2022-11 at +2.97 and 2025-05 at +2.14) are safely below the threshold, so they're kept.

The name "K" is just the variable name for the threshold value — `K=12` means the cutoff is 12. The gap in the data between `n_c25=11` and `n_c25=14` means K=12 and K=13 give identical results, which makes it robust — you're not balancing on a knife edge.

Honest answer: **it is NOT mathematically grounded. It is a post-hoc pattern observation dressed up with a theoretical story.** Let me reason this out carefully.

---

## What it actually is

**The sequence of events:**
1. We ran 23 folds and observed the results
2. We then looked at the n_c25 values and the SRs together
3. We noticed that all 6 folds where n_c25 > 12 happened to be negative
4. We called K=12 a "natural gap" and said it's theoretically motivated

That is data mining, not a pipeline construct.

---

## Why the theoretical story is incomplete

The economic argument — "high n_c25 means factor inflation, which means bad trading" — is internally consistent with the research doc. But the theory only says **direction** (more pairs = more factor exposure risk). The theory says nothing about where the threshold should be. It does not say:

- K should be 12 and not 8 or 20
- That the relationship is a hard binary step function at K, not a continuous degradation
- That K=12 would hold in a different sample with different market conditions

The "natural gap" between n_c25=11 and n_c25=14 is a property of our specific 45-fold schedule on our specific universe in this specific time period. It has no mathematical necessity. In another dataset, there could easily be a fold with n_c25=12 that is positive, which would invalidate the rule entirely.

---

## The statistical evidence is very weak

With 6 folds above the threshold, all negative:

```
P(6/6 negative | baseline negative rate 48%) = 0.48^6 ≈ 1.2%
```

Superficially significant. But:

**1. The observations are not independent.** The 6 bad folds cluster heavily in 2025-2026 (folds 38, 39, 40) and in the same late-bull macro environment. They are effectively 2-3 correlated regime events, not 6 independent draws. The true effective N is much smaller than 6.

**2. The threshold was chosen after seeing the data.** If we had 20 candidate thresholds to test, the most extreme split would appear significant by chance. Bonferroni-correcting for multiple testing makes 1.2% much less impressive.

**3. Small-universe bad folds exist.** Folds 32, 43, 44 (n_c25 = 2, 5, 5) are also negative. The theory predicts large n_c25 = bad, but it cannot explain why n_c25=5 is sometimes bad and sometimes good. The direction is right but the signal is noisy even in-sample.

---

## The research doc already warned us about this exact class of fix

Fix C from the doc:

> *"Almost no degrees of freedom. Equivalent to in-sample regime selection. PBO will explode."*

The n_c25 cap is Fix C implemented with an internal signal instead of a market signal. The fundamental problem is identical: **a fold-level binary gate on 23 folds has essentially 1 effective hyperparameter consuming most of the available variance.** The research doc rejected Fix C as a first test for exactly this reason. We've now arrived at the same class of fix from a different angle.

---

## What IS grounded

The **direction** of the signal is grounded:
- High n_c25 → more pairs passed Johansen under factor co-movement → formation universe is more factor-inflated → higher expected drift in trading window
- This is consistent with Avellaneda & Lee (2010) and the research doc's mechanism

The **monotonicity** is grounded: there is no reason to believe the relationship reverses at some point. Worse is worse.

What is NOT grounded: the specific threshold K=12, the binary step function, the claim that K=12 would generalize out-of-sample.

---

## The honest verdict

| Claim | Status |
|---|---|
| High n_c25 predicts worse outcomes | Theoretically motivated, directionally correct |
| The relationship is strong enough to act on | NOT established — 6 clustered observations |
| K=12 is the right threshold | Pure data mining, no mathematical basis |
| This is Fix C in disguise | Yes — the research doc already assessed and deferred this class |
| Out-of-sample reliability | Unknown — requires future folds to validate |

**The correct framing:** The n_c25 direction is a useful diagnostic finding to document in the whitepaper as a hypothesis. It should be presented as: *"In our dataset, folds with n_c25 > 12 were uniformly negative, consistent with the factor-inflation mechanism. This warrants further investigation in future data."* It should NOT be applied as a production filter without out-of-sample validation.

**The bottom line:** We have a theoretically coherent story and a consistent in-sample observation with too few degrees of freedom to treat as a validated rule. Acting on K=12 would be in-sample overfitting — exactly what the research doc warned against for Fix C.

CORR25 remains the best validated configuration. The n_c25 pattern is a research finding for the whitepaper, not a filter to add to the pipeline.

The NC is artificially constrained to EOS exits, making it slightly worse than if it used no-EOS. This biases the NC discrimination test in the primary's favor — NC pass rates are slightly inflated. The audit log's RED FLAG fires on 12/23 folds but for the wrong comparison.

The results doc note that says "measurement artifact" is now precisely explained.

### Assistant `2026-05-03 01:11:12`
No — the two diagnostics say different things, and the warning label is misleading for this case.

**DSR = 0.00** is not really a meaningful overfitting signal here. DSR asks: *"Is the observed Sharpe statistically above zero after adjusting for multiple trials?"* But the raw annualized Sharpe computed from daily returns is already **−1.42** — it's negative to start with. DSR being zero just reflects that the strategy loses money on average, not that it was tuned to historical data. The "likely overfit" label triggers whenever DSR < 0.05, which is a poor fit for a losing strategy.

**PBO = 0.057 (5.7%)** is the more meaningful number, and it's actually a good result. PBO asks: *"In combinatorial cross-validation, how often does the in-sample winner underperform out-of-sample?"* At 5.7%, the strategy is well below the 0.50 threshold that would indicate overfitting. The signal generalizes across walk-forward folds — it's not picking up noise from curve-fitting.

So the honest read is:
- **Not overfit** (PBO = 5.7%) — the walk-forward structure is sound
- **Losing strategy** (mean Sharpe −0.516) — the edge is real but insufficient to overcome the Bull 2025 regime collapse

The DSR warning is a false alarm caused by negative returns feeding into a formula designed for positive-Sharpe strategies. If you want, I can add a note to the results doc clarifying this distinction so it doesn't confuse readers of the whitepaper.

Done. Here are the full §6 structural results:

**Z_entry sweep** (all 23 folds):

| Z_entry | Mean SR | Δ vs 3.0 | % Pos |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.50 | −1.101 | −0.585 | 39% |
| 2.75 | −1.005 | −0.489 | 35% |
| **3.00 (default)** | **−0.516** | — | **48%** |
| 3.25 | −0.295 | +0.221 | 43% |
| 3.50 | −0.474 | +0.042 | 39% |

**Stop-loss sweep** (N=21 — 2 zero-trade folds produce NaN from the rolling bar calc):

| Stop-loss | Mean SR | Δ vs None | % Pos |
|---|---|---|---|
| **None (default)** | **−0.516** | — | **48%** |
| −2.5% | −0.263 | +0.253 | 52% |
| −5.0% | −0.703 | −0.187 | 52% |

**Key findings:**

1. **Z=3.0 is the right choice.** It has the highest % positive (48%) of any Z value. Z=3.25 has a better mean SR (−0.295 vs −0.516) but lower % positive (43%) — 1 fold difference on 23 folds, well within noise. Anything below Z=3.0 is materially worse (more trades = more TC drag).

2. **SL −2.5% apparent improvement is real but has a caveat.** It shows +0.253 mean SR improvement and 52% positive. However N=21 vs N=23 — the 2 missing folds are the zero-trade folds (SR=0.0). On a like-for-like N=21 basis, the default SR would be −0.565, so the gap is genuinely +0.302. This conflicts with the earlier stop-loss experiment (+−0.351 delta). The difference: **different implementations** — the earlier test used a flat $400/trade threshold; this uses a rolling 5-bar PnL window. These are not directly comparable. Given the conflict, stop-loss remains inconclusive rather than definitively helpful or harmful.

3. **SL −5.0% hurts** (−0.187 delta). The threshold is too loose — only fires on catastrophic 5% losses in 5 bars, missing the moderately bad trades that are the real drag.

**Bottom line:** Z=3.0 confirmed as the correct default. Stop-loss at −2.5% with a 5-bar rolling window is a candidate for further investigation, but the methodology conflict with the earlier experiment means it can't be applied without a cleaner controlled test.

### Assistant `2026-05-03 02:05:00`
Good question. The answer is **mostly yes**, but with one important caveat about what data you actually have.

**Why post-hoc ≈ in-pipeline here:**
- Position sizing is fixed dollar ($20,000/pair from $1M/50) — not equity-scaled. So excluding a trade doesn't change the capital base for subsequent trades. No compounding distortion.
- With 2–19 trades per fold and N_max=50, the concentration cap is never binding. Rejecting an entry doesn't free a slot that changes another trade.
- A rejected entry means no TC charged for entry or exit — the post-hoc can replicate this exactly by removing those trades' P&L and TC from the fold.

**The real problem — you don't have what you need:**
The Z-velocity at entry requires `Z[entry_ts - K bars]`. The current trade logs store `entry_ts`, `gross_pnl`, `net_pnl`, `exit_reason` — but **not the Z-score series**. The engine output (`pair_df`) has `position`, `beta_post`, `rebalance_cost` — also no Z-score column saved.

So to do this post-hoc you'd need to either:

1. **Re-run Kalman + rolling Z-score for each pair** (fast — just signal generation, skip the state machine), load the Z series, look up `Z[entry_ts]` and `Z[entry_ts - K bars]`, compute velocity. This is ~95% of a full rerun and the result would match the in-pipeline version almost exactly.

2. **Modify the engine to save the Z-score column** in its output DataFrame, then rerun. This is the cleanest approach — one-line change, then the post-hoc test is trivially just a filter on the trade log.

**Bottom line:** Option 2 is the right path. Add `z_score` to the engine output, rerun `run_final_pipeline.py` (same 23 folds, ~same runtime as the original), then the post-hoc filter on entry Z-velocity gives results identical to an in-pipeline implementation. You avoid touching the Numba JIT state machine itself until you've confirmed the threshold is worth it.

### Assistant `2026-05-03 02:12:38`
The audit logs only have fold-level averages, not per-trade distributions. Here's what the data shows — and why you'd need a rerun with trade logging to get the exact percentage:

**What we can see (fold-level averages):**

| | Value |
|---|---|
| Avg holding period | 2.24 days |
| Avg pair HL (median, post-cap) | 3.33 days |
| Avg hold as % of HL | **~67%** |

So on average, trades exit at roughly **two-thirds of the HL** — meaning the *typical* trade closes before the spread is even halfway reverted. That sounds like a problem, but it's actually correct behavior: if the spread reverts fully to zero (zero-cross), it exits *before* the HL by definition (zero-cross happens faster than HL predicts when reversion is strong).

**The concerning folds are where avg hold exceeds the HL:**

| Fold | Avg Hold | Median HL | Hold/HL | Sharpe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11 (May 2023) | 3.35d | 2.89d | **116%** | −1.70 |
| 2 (Aug 2022) | 3.25d | 2.62d | **124%** | +3.69 |
| 32 (Feb 2025) | 3.45d | 3.17d | **109%** | −2.36 |
| 12 (Jun 2023) | 3.21d | 3.23d | 99% | −5.64 |

Fold 2 is the exception — it went past HL and still profited. Folds 11, 12, 32 went past HL and lost.

**Bottom line:** To get the exact per-trade percentage you'd need to save `n_bars` per trade in the pipeline. But from the fold-level data, my estimate is roughly **25–35% of trades exceed their pair's HL** — concentrated almost entirely in the Late Bull 2025 and the two spike folds (11, 12). In the Bear and Early Bull positive folds, trades are exiting well within the HL.

Results are in. Clean comparison:

| Metric | TC=30 bps/leg | TC=15 bps/leg | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mean Sharpe | −0.516 | **+0.295** | **+0.811** |
| Median Sharpe | 0.000 | **+0.525** | **+0.525** |
| % Positive | 48% | 52% | +4pp |
| NC pass rate | 8.7% (2/23) | **17.4% (4/23)** | +8.7pp |
| Commission | $55,627 | $27,813 | −50% |
| Bear SR | +1.357 | +1.733 | +0.376 |
| Early Bull SR | −0.032 | **+0.944** | +0.976 |
| Mid Bull SR | −0.179 | **+0.913** | +1.092 |
| Late Bull SR | −1.811 | **−0.938** | +0.873 |

**Key takeaways:**

1. **Mean SR crosses zero (+0.295) — the strategy is marginally net-positive at 15 bps/leg.** Median of +0.525 is more meaningful given fold 40 is a structural outlier.

2. **Every regime improves by ~+0.9 SR.** The TC drag is uniformly distributed across regimes. But the Late Bull is still the only regime that remains negative (−0.938) — confirming that's a gross P&L failure, not TC.

3. **The persistently bad folds don't change much.** Fold 12: −5.64 → −5.01. Fold 40: −4.98 → −5.01 (barely moves — gross loss dominates). Fold 38: −4.77 → −2.85 (TC was meaningful here). These folds are losing on gross P&L before TC.

4. **Several marginal folds flip.** Fold 36: −0.49 → +0.53. Fold 37: +0.03 → +0.94. Fold 23: −2.19 → −0.40 (nearly breaks even).

**Bottom line:** At 15 bps/leg the strategy has a positive mean Sharpe. The 30 bps/leg assumption was overly conservative for the filtered 150-trade universe. Whether 15 bps is actually achievable depends on execution infrastructure — but this confirms TC is still a meaningful lever even after the CORR25 filter.

## Audit Findings

### ISSUE 1 — Critical: CORR25 attribution is backwards

**Claim (multiple locations):** "CORR25 was the primary driver of the 99.7% trade count reduction."

**What the code shows:** `n_gate = n_corr` in **all 23 completed folds** — CORR25 removed zero pairs within any fold that survived to that step. Its only contribution was eliminating 7 entire folds where *all* remaining pairs failed the correlation floor.

The persistence gate is the actual primary within-fold filter. It alone drove the spike-fold collapses: 1,921 → 37 (Fold 11), 6,008 → 27 (Fold 23), 5,913 → 29 (Fold 40). That 98%+ reduction within those three folds accounts for the bulk of the 43,453 → 150 trade drop.

Correct attribution: persistence gate = primary driver of trade count reduction; CORR25 = eliminated 7 additional folds entirely; Z=3.0 = further reduced trades per pair within surviving folds.

---

### ISSUE 2 — Critical: §2.3 pipeline steps are wrong scope

**Claim:** Steps 6 (persistence gate) and 7 (CORR25) are listed as standard pair-selection steps alongside Steps 1–5.

**What the code shows:** `discovery.py` implements only Steps 1–5. Steps 6 and 7 live in `run_final_pipeline.py` — they are Option A post-processors applied after Phase 1 output is loaded. A quant reading §2.3 would assume these are in Phase 1 and go looking for them in the wrong place.

Additionally, Step 5 says HL ∈ [1, **6**] days, but `discovery.py` uses `_HL_MAX_DAYS = 10.0`. The [1,6] cap is applied separately in `run_final_pipeline.py` as a post-Phase-1 filter.

---

### ISSUE 3 — Significant: Kalman economic rationale contradicts its actual behavior

**Claim (§1.1):** "A Kalman filter allows the hedge ratio to drift slowly over time as the fundamental relationship between two stocks evolves."

**What the code shows:** δ = 1e-7 in 100% of folds. Q = δ·R·I₂ produces near-zero Kalman gain — the filter barely adapts from its PCA initialization. §3.1 correctly calls it "near-static." §1.1 implies active adaptation as part of the investment thesis, which is not what the implementation delivers. A committee member who reads §1.1 then looks at §3.1 and §11 will notice the contradiction immediately.

---

### ISSUE 4 — Significant: CORR25 computed on log-returns, not log-prices

**Claim (§1.3 and §2.3):** "full-formation-window Pearson correlation ≥ 0.25"

**What the code shows:** `run_final_pipeline.py` lines 199–223 compute `ra.corr(rb)` where `ra` and `rb` are log-return series, not log-price series. These are materially different. Two trending stocks can have very high price correlation but low return correlation. Return correlation is the more conservative and statistically appropriate measure. The whitepaper should say "log-return correlation."

---

### ISSUE 5 — Moderate: NC "confirms statistical significance" is too strong

**Claim (§6.4):** "The NC test confirms statistical significance in Bear regime."

**What the data shows:** NC pass rate = 2/23 folds (8.7%). One of the two passing folds (Fold 2) is based on **1 trade**. A single winning trade generating a high Sharpe that beats the NC threshold is not statistical significance in any conventional sense. "Provides limited evidence" or "passes the NC threshold in the strategy's two strongest folds" is defensible. "Confirms" is not.

---

### ISSUE 6 — Moderate: Bear "60% positive" obscures zero-trade folds

**Claim (§5.2, §5.4):** Bear regime: 5 folds, 60% positive, mean SR +1.357.

**What the data shows:** Folds 3 and 6 have SR = 0.000 because they have **zero trades** (1 pair each, none triggered at Z=3.0). The mean SR of +1.357 is built entirely on 17 trades across Folds 1, 2, and 5. The committee will ask why two Bear folds produced no trades — and the answer (1 pair each, Z=3.0 never triggered) should be in the paper, not discovered under questioning.

---

### ISSUE 7 — Moderate: TC breakeven is an interpolation, not a measurement

**Claim (§6.2):** "Breakeven TC is approximately 20–25 bps per leg."

**What was measured:** TC=30 bps/leg → SR −0.516; TC=15 bps/leg → SR +0.295. The 20–25 bps figure is a linear interpolation between two points. Linear interpolation between Sharpe values is not reliable (SR is nonlinear in TC because trade count is constant but the distribution of winners vs losers shifts). Should be stated as "estimated by interpolation between the two measured points" rather than stated as a fact.

---

### ISSUE 8 — Minor: Mid Bull 2024 regime inference should be disclaimed harder

**Claim (§5.2):** Mid Bull 2024: 2 completed folds, 50% positive.

**What the data shows:** Fold 20 (+1.830, 3 trades) and Fold 23 (−2.188, 11 trades). This is 14 total trades from 2 folds. "50% positive" from two data points is not a regime finding. The table lists it with IQR "—" which is correct, but the regime comparison table presenting it alongside Bear (5 folds) and Late Bull (10 folds) implies comparability that doesn't exist.

---

### ISSUE 9 — Minor: §1.1 economic rationale implies sector constraint that doesn't exist

**Claim (§1.1):** "Pairs in the same sector, supply chain, or competitive landscape are exposed to common macro shocks."

**What the code shows:** `discovery.py` has no sector filter. The pair universe is all-pairs across the full screened S&P 500 — two names from completely unrelated industries can and do pair. The economic rationale in §1.1 describes the *ideal* case, not the actual selection. A committee member might ask "so how do you enforce the economic rationale?" and the honest answer is: the strategy doesn't; it relies entirely on the statistical tests.

## Tier 1: Affects every Sharpe in the whitepaper

### **BUG-1: Sharpe annualization includes weekend/holiday zero-bars**
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:247-252`
```python
daily_pnl     = bar_pnl.resample("D").sum()   # creates Sat/Sun bins with sum=0
daily_returns = daily_pnl / total_capital
sharpe = float(daily_returns.mean() / std_daily * np.sqrt(252))
```
`resample("D")` produces a regular calendar-day index from min to max of `bar_pnl.index`, including weekends and holidays. Those days are filled with `sum()` of nothing = 0. For a 1-month fold (~22 trading days, ~30 calendar days), this dilutes mean by ~5/7 and shifts std toward zero-mass. **Every Sharpe in the whitepaper is biased.** Fix: `resample("B")` or `groupby(idx.normalize())` then drop empty days.
**Severity: Critical — affects every reported Sharpe magnitude.**

### **BUG-2: CAGR uses calendar days, not trading days**
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:256`
```python
n_days = len(daily_returns)   # calendar days from resample("D")
cagr   = (1.0 + total_ret) ** (252.0 / max(n_days, 1)) - 1.0
```
For a 30-calendar-day fold with 22 trading days, the exponent is 252/30 = 8.4 instead of correct 252/22 = 11.5. CAGR magnitude understated by ~30%. Calmar (= CAGR / |MaxDD|) inherits the bug.
**Severity: Critical for any CAGR/Calmar number in the paper.**

### **BUG-3: Negative-β pairs produce wrong P&L (β-sign cascade)**
`src/phase1_cointegration/discovery.py:165` admits any sign of β.
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:105,117`:
```python
shares_b = (short_notional * abs(beta[i - 1])) / p_b   # sizing uses |β|
gross    = direction * (shares_a * dp_a - shares_b * dp_b)   # but always minus on B
```
Verified: there is **no `beta_pca > 0` filter anywhere** (grep across all phase modules and `run_final_pipeline.py`). For β<0 pairs the PCA cointegrating combination is `ln(A) + |β|·ln(B)` — both legs same direction — but the PnL trades A long / B short regardless of sign. Sign-wrong on entire trade P&L for any negative-β pair admitted.
**Severity: Critical contingent on incidence.** Need to count: how many of the 150 final-config trades came from β<0 pairs? If any, those trades' P&L has the wrong sign.

---

## Tier 2: Affects specific defenses in the whitepaper

### **BUG-4: NC bootstrap uses block_size=1 (= i.i.d. bootstrap, not block bootstrap)**
`src/phase3_backtest/neg_control.py:250`
```python
def _block_bootstrap_sharpe(daily_returns, n_bootstrap=1000, block_size=1, seed=42):
```
Default `block_size=1` collapses block bootstrap to standard i.i.d. bootstrap. Pipeline spec §3.5 explicitly requires block bootstrap (block_size = 1 day = 390 bars) to preserve serial correlation. With i.i.d. resampling, the NC bootstrap variance is underestimated → NC threshold too tight → strategy "passes" too easily. The 8.7% (2/23) NC pass rate is likely inflated relative to a correct block bootstrap (real number could be 0/23).
**Severity: Significant — undercuts the NC defense in §6.4.**

### **BUG-5: Same NC seed (42) reused across all folds**
`neg_control.py:251` — bootstrap uses `seed=42` regardless of fold. NC distributions across folds are perfectly correlated (same draws). Independent fold-level NC tests are needed for any cross-fold NC aggregation.
**Severity: Minor — affects fold-level NC pass rate aggregation only.**

### **BUG-6: Latency convention is aggressive (decide-at-close = fill-at-close)**
`engine.py:241` shifts position by 1 bar; `pnl.py:102` then prices the fill at `ca[i-1]`.
- Engine: position[i] = signal[i-1] (1-bar position shift)
- PnL: entry fill at price[i-1] (= signal bar's close)

Net effect: signal generation and execution happen at the same bar's close → **zero net latency**. The latency.py sweep then tests t+1, t+5 *on top of* this already-zero-latency baseline. The whitepaper §6.5 latency claim ("0/23 folds latency-robust") is measured against a baseline that has no latency to begin with.
**Severity: Significant — defensible convention but should be disclosed.**

---

## Tier 3: Logic divergences from spec

### **BUG-7: No fold-boundary position carry-forward**
`engine.py:241` initializes `position = np.zeros(n)` per fold. `run_final_pipeline.py` does not feed open positions across fold boundaries. CLAUDE.md §"Rolling Walk-Forward Architecture" explicitly says: *"Fold boundary: open positions carry forward to natural exit (zero-cross)."*
**Severity: Significant — direct spec/code divergence. The whitepaper §4.1 lists this as a methodology feature; the code does not implement it.**

### **BUG-8: CORR25 `.diff()` produces returns that span overnight gaps**
`run_final_pipeline.py:215-218`
```python
ra = aln["log_close_a"].diff()   # diff over inner-joined irregular index
rb = aln["log_close_b"].diff()
```
After `inner_join` and any NaN dropping, consecutive rows can span session boundaries (15:55 → 09:35 next day = 17h40m gap). Those overnight "returns" are mixed into a Pearson correlation calibrated as if all gaps were 5 min. Distorts the 0.25 threshold meaning.
**Severity: Significant — the entire CORR25 narrative depends on the 0.25 floor being a meaningful number.**

### **BUG-9: Engine rebalance share count off by factor of |β|**
`engine.py:267`
```python
delta_shares_b = abs(delta_beta) * (short_notional / max(close_b_1min[i], 1e-6))
```
`short_notional` in the engine = `per_pair_dollar * 0.5`. But in `pnl.py:105`, the actual short-side shares are `short_notional * |β| / p_b`. So the actual short notional invested is `|β| × short_notional`, and rebalance shares should scale with that. Rebalance cost off by factor |β|.
**Severity: Minor in final config (total rebalance = $153 across 23 folds), but a defensibility issue.**

### **BUG-10: Borrow cost timing**
`pnl.py:122-129` charges borrow on `shares_b * cb[i]` (today's price at first bar of new session) instead of yesterday's close (correct overnight accrual base). Also, entry day's partial accrual is missing entirely (entry sets `prev_date = curr_date`, so first new-day check fires only on day 2).
**Severity: Minor in final config (total borrow = $354), but accounting is wrong.**

---

## Tier 4: Statistical / robustness

### **BUG-11: Persistence gate's Johansen has a 20-bar minimum (way too low)**
`run_final_pipeline.py:181-194` — re-runs Johansen on the last month of formation. Minimum-overlap floor of 20 bars is order-of-magnitude too low for a Johansen test (which needs 100+ obs minimum for the chi2 approximation to hold). In practice the last-month window contains ~1700 5-min bars so this floor rarely binds, but for sparse pairs it could admit unreliable p-values.
**Severity: Minor — practical impact small.**

### **BUG-12: Trade-level `net_pnl` excludes exit-bar rebalance cost**
`pnl.py:146` computes `trade_net_pnl = bar_pnl[entry_bar:i+1].sum()` *before* line 166 deducts `reb_cost[i]` from `bar_pnl[i]`. So the rebalance cost on the exit bar enters the aggregate `bar_pnl` but is missing from per-trade `net_pnl`. The §6.5 exit-reason analytics ("avg net bps") slightly overstate per-trade profitability for trades that had a rebalance on the exit bar.
**Severity: Minor — affects per-trade analytics, not aggregate.**

---

5. BUG-7 (no carry-forward) is a documentation fix or an implementation fix. Pick one. The whitepaper currently claims walk-forward with carry-forward; the code starts each fold flat. They must agree.

I would not deliver the whitepaper to the boss before BUG-1, BUG-2, and the BUG-3 incidence count are resolved. The other items can be disclosed honestly without rerunning.

## Audit Findings

### ISSUE 1 — Critical: CORR25 attribution is backwards

**Claim (multiple locations):** "CORR25 was the primary driver of the 99.7% trade count reduction."

**What the code shows:** `n_gate = n_corr` in **all 23 completed folds** — CORR25 removed zero pairs within any fold that survived to that step. Its only contribution was eliminating 7 entire folds where *all* remaining pairs failed the correlation floor.

The persistence gate is the actual primary within-fold filter. It alone drove the spike-fold collapses: 1,921 → 37 (Fold 11), 6,008 → 27 (Fold 23), 5,913 → 29 (Fold 40). That 98%+ reduction within those three folds accounts for the bulk of the 43,453 → 150 trade drop.

Correct attribution: persistence gate = primary driver of trade count reduction; CORR25 = eliminated 7 additional folds entirely; Z=3.0 = further reduced trades per pair within surviving folds.

---

### ISSUE 2 — Critical: §2.3 pipeline steps are wrong scope

**Claim:** Steps 6 (persistence gate) and 7 (CORR25) are listed as standard pair-selection steps alongside Steps 1–5.

**What the code shows:** `discovery.py` implements only Steps 1–5. Steps 6 and 7 live in `run_final_pipeline.py` — they are Option A post-processors applied after Phase 1 output is loaded. A quant reading §2.3 would assume these are in Phase 1 and go looking for them in the wrong place.

Additionally, Step 5 says HL ∈ [1, **6**] days, but `discovery.py` uses `_HL_MAX_DAYS = 10.0`. The [1,6] cap is applied separately in `run_final_pipeline.py` as a post-Phase-1 filter.

---

### ISSUE 3 — Significant: Kalman economic rationale contradicts its actual behavior

**Claim (§1.1):** "A Kalman filter allows the hedge ratio to drift slowly over time as the fundamental relationship between two stocks evolves."

**What the code shows:** δ = 1e-7 in 100% of folds. Q = δ·R·I₂ produces near-zero Kalman gain — the filter barely adapts from its PCA initialization. §3.1 correctly calls it "near-static." §1.1 implies active adaptation as part of the investment thesis, which is not what the implementation delivers. A committee member who reads §1.1 then looks at §3.1 and §11 will notice the contradiction immediately.

---

### ISSUE 4 — Significant: CORR25 computed on log-returns, not log-prices

**Claim (§1.3 and §2.3):** "full-formation-window Pearson correlation ≥ 0.25"

**What the code shows:** `run_final_pipeline.py` lines 199–223 compute `ra.corr(rb)` where `ra` and `rb` are log-return series, not log-price series. These are materially different. Two trending stocks can have very high price correlation but low return correlation. Return correlation is the more conservative and statistically appropriate measure. The whitepaper should say "log-return correlation."

---

### ISSUE 5 — Moderate: NC "confirms statistical significance" is too strong

**Claim (§6.4):** "The NC test confirms statistical significance in Bear regime."

**What the data shows:** NC pass rate = 2/23 folds (8.7%). One of the two passing folds (Fold 2) is based on **1 trade**. A single winning trade generating a high Sharpe that beats the NC threshold is not statistical significance in any conventional sense. "Provides limited evidence" or "passes the NC threshold in the strategy's two strongest folds" is defensible. "Confirms" is not.

---

### ISSUE 6 — Moderate: Bear "60% positive" obscures zero-trade folds

**Claim (§5.2, §5.4):** Bear regime: 5 folds, 60% positive, mean SR +1.357.

**What the data shows:** Folds 3 and 6 have SR = 0.000 because they have **zero trades** (1 pair each, none triggered at Z=3.0). The mean SR of +1.357 is built entirely on 17 trades across Folds 1, 2, and 5. The committee will ask why two Bear folds produced no trades — and the answer (1 pair each, Z=3.0 never triggered) should be in the paper, not discovered under questioning.

---

### ISSUE 7 — Moderate: TC breakeven is an interpolation, not a measurement

**Claim (§6.2):** "Breakeven TC is approximately 20–25 bps per leg."

**What was measured:** TC=30 bps/leg → SR −0.516; TC=15 bps/leg → SR +0.295. The 20–25 bps figure is a linear interpolation between two points. Linear interpolation between Sharpe values is not reliable (SR is nonlinear in TC because trade count is constant but the distribution of winners vs losers shifts). Should be stated as "estimated by interpolation between the two measured points" rather than stated as a fact.

---

### ISSUE 8 — Minor: Mid Bull 2024 regime inference should be disclaimed harder

**Claim (§5.2):** Mid Bull 2024: 2 completed folds, 50% positive.

**What the data shows:** Fold 20 (+1.830, 3 trades) and Fold 23 (−2.188, 11 trades). This is 14 total trades from 2 folds. "50% positive" from two data points is not a regime finding. The table lists it with IQR "—" which is correct, but the regime comparison table presenting it alongside Bear (5 folds) and Late Bull (10 folds) implies comparability that doesn't exist.

---

### ISSUE 9 — Minor: §1.1 economic rationale implies sector constraint that doesn't exist

**Claim (§1.1):** "Pairs in the same sector, supply chain, or competitive landscape are exposed to common macro shocks."

**What the code shows:** `discovery.py` has no sector filter. The pair universe is all-pairs across the full screened S&P 500 — two names from completely unrelated industries can and do pair. The economic rationale in §1.1 describes the *ideal* case, not the actual selection. A committee member might ask "so how do you enforce the economic rationale?" and the honest answer is: the strategy doesn't; it relies entirely on the statistical tests.

## Tier 1: Affects every Sharpe in the whitepaper

### **BUG-1: Sharpe annualization includes weekend/holiday zero-bars**
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:247-252`
```python
daily_pnl     = bar_pnl.resample("D").sum()   # creates Sat/Sun bins with sum=0
daily_returns = daily_pnl / total_capital
sharpe = float(daily_returns.mean() / std_daily * np.sqrt(252))
```
`resample("D")` produces a regular calendar-day index from min to max of `bar_pnl.index`, including weekends and holidays. Those days are filled with `sum()` of nothing = 0. For a 1-month fold (~22 trading days, ~30 calendar days), this dilutes mean by ~5/7 and shifts std toward zero-mass. **Every Sharpe in the whitepaper is biased.** Fix: `resample("B")` or `groupby(idx.normalize())` then drop empty days.
**Severity: Critical — affects every reported Sharpe magnitude.**

### **BUG-2: CAGR uses calendar days, not trading days**
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:256`
```python
n_days = len(daily_returns)   # calendar days from resample("D")
cagr   = (1.0 + total_ret) ** (252.0 / max(n_days, 1)) - 1.0
```
For a 30-calendar-day fold with 22 trading days, the exponent is 252/30 = 8.4 instead of correct 252/22 = 11.5. CAGR magnitude understated by ~30%. Calmar (= CAGR / |MaxDD|) inherits the bug.
**Severity: Critical for any CAGR/Calmar number in the paper.**

### **BUG-3: Negative-β pairs produce wrong P&L (β-sign cascade)**
`src/phase1_cointegration/discovery.py:165` admits any sign of β.
`src/phase3_backtest/pnl.py:105,117`:
```python
shares_b = (short_notional * abs(beta[i - 1])) / p_b   # sizing uses |β|
gross    = direction * (shares_a * dp_a - shares_b * dp_b)   # but always minus on B
```
Verified: there is **no `beta_pca > 0` filter anywhere** (grep across all phase modules and `run_final_pipeline.py`). For β<0 pairs the PCA cointegrating combination is `ln(A) + |β|·ln(B)` — both legs same direction — but the PnL trades A long / B short regardless of sign. Sign-wrong on entire trade P&L for any negative-β pair admitted.
**Severity: Critical contingent on incidence.** Need to count: how many of the 150 final-config trades came from β<0 pairs? If any, those trades' P&L has the wrong sign.

---

## Tier 2: Affects specific defenses in the whitepaper

### **BUG-4: NC bootstrap uses block_size=1 (= i.i.d. bootstrap, not block bootstrap)**
`src/phase3_backtest/neg_control.py:250`
```python
def _block_bootstrap_sharpe(daily_returns, n_bootstrap=1000, block_size=1, seed=42):
```
Default `block_size=1` collapses block bootstrap to standard i.i.d. bootstrap. Pipeline spec §3.5 explicitly requires block bootstrap (block_size = 1 day = 390 bars) to preserve serial correlation. With i.i.d. resampling, the NC bootstrap variance is underestimated → NC threshold too tight → strategy "passes" too easily. The 8.7% (2/23) NC pass rate is likely inflated relative to a correct block bootstrap (real number could be 0/23).
**Severity: Significant — undercuts the NC defense in §6.4.**

### **BUG-5: Same NC seed (42) reused across all folds**
`neg_control.py:251` — bootstrap uses `seed=42` regardless of fold. NC distributions across folds are perfectly correlated (same draws). Independent fold-level NC tests are needed for any cross-fold NC aggregation.
**Severity: Minor — affects fold-level NC pass rate aggregation only.**

### **BUG-6: Latency convention is aggressive (decide-at-close = fill-at-close)**
`engine.py:241` shifts position by 1 bar; `pnl.py:102` then prices the fill at `ca[i-1]`.
- Engine: position[i] = signal[i-1] (1-bar position shift)
- PnL: entry fill at price[i-1] (= signal bar's close)

Net effect: signal generation and execution happen at the same bar's close → **zero net latency**. The latency.py sweep then tests t+1, t+5 *on top of* this already-zero-latency baseline. The whitepaper §6.5 latency claim ("0/23 folds latency-robust") is measured against a baseline that has no latency to begin with.
**Severity: Significant — defensible convention but should be disclosed.**

---

## Tier 3: Logic divergences from spec

### **BUG-7: No fold-boundary position carry-forward**
`engine.py:241` initializes `position = np.zeros(n)` per fold. `run_final_pipeline.py` does not feed open positions across fold boundaries. CLAUDE.md §"Rolling Walk-Forward Architecture" explicitly says: *"Fold boundary: open positions carry forward to natural exit (zero-cross)."*
**Severity: Significant — direct spec/code divergence. The whitepaper §4.1 lists this as a methodology feature; the code does not implement it.**

### **BUG-8: CORR25 `.diff()` produces returns that span overnight gaps**
`run_final_pipeline.py:215-218`
```python
ra = aln["log_close_a"].diff()   # diff over inner-joined irregular index
rb = aln["log_close_b"].diff()
```
After `inner_join` and any NaN dropping, consecutive rows can span session boundaries (15:55 → 09:35 next day = 17h40m gap). Those overnight "returns" are mixed into a Pearson correlation calibrated as if all gaps were 5 min. Distorts the 0.25 threshold meaning.
**Severity: Significant — the entire CORR25 narrative depends on the 0.25 floor being a meaningful number.**

### **BUG-9: Engine rebalance share count off by factor of |β|**
`engine.py:267`
```python
delta_shares_b = abs(delta_beta) * (short_notional / max(close_b_1min[i], 1e-6))
```
`short_notional` in the engine = `per_pair_dollar * 0.5`. But in `pnl.py:105`, the actual short-side shares are `short_notional * |β| / p_b`. So the actual short notional invested is `|β| × short_notional`, and rebalance shares should scale with that. Rebalance cost off by factor |β|.
**Severity: Minor in final config (total rebalance = $153 across 23 folds), but a defensibility issue.**

### **BUG-10: Borrow cost timing**
`pnl.py:122-129` charges borrow on `shares_b * cb[i]` (today's price at first bar of new session) instead of yesterday's close (correct overnight accrual base). Also, entry day's partial accrual is missing entirely (entry sets `prev_date = curr_date`, so first new-day check fires only on day 2).
**Severity: Minor in final config (total borrow = $354), but accounting is wrong.**

---

## Tier 4: Statistical / robustness

### **BUG-11: Persistence gate's Johansen has a 20-bar minimum (way too low)**
`run_final_pipeline.py:181-194` — re-runs Johansen on the last month of formation. Minimum-overlap floor of 20 bars is order-of-magnitude too low for a Johansen test (which needs 100+ obs minimum for the chi2 approximation to hold). In practice the last-month window contains ~1700 5-min bars so this floor rarely binds, but for sparse pairs it could admit unreliable p-values.
**Severity: Minor — practical impact small.**

### **BUG-12: Trade-level `net_pnl` excludes exit-bar rebalance cost**
`pnl.py:146` computes `trade_net_pnl = bar_pnl[entry_bar:i+1].sum()` *before* line 166 deducts `reb_cost[i]` from `bar_pnl[i]`. So the rebalance cost on the exit bar enters the aggregate `bar_pnl` but is missing from per-trade `net_pnl`. The §6.5 exit-reason analytics ("avg net bps") slightly overstate per-trade profitability for trades that had a rebalance on the exit bar.
**Severity: Minor — affects per-trade analytics, not aggregate.**

---

3. Decide whether to disclose BUG-6 (latency convention) explicitly in the whitepaper. The honest framing is: "fills are at the signal bar's close; the latency sweep tests t+1/t+5 on top of this baseline."

4. BUG-4 (NC bootstrap) — flip default `block_size=5` (or higher) and rerun NC; expect the 2/23 pass rate to drop, possibly to 0/23. This will require an honest update to §6.4.

5. BUG-7 (no carry-forward) is a documentation fix or an implementation fix. Pick one. The whitepaper currently claims walk-forward with carry-forward; the code starts each fold flat. They must agree.

I would not deliver the whitepaper to the boss before BUG-1, BUG-2, and the BUG-3 incidence count are resolved. The other items can be disclosed honestly without rerunning.

### Assistant `2026-05-03 05:15:04`
Now adding `side_A`/`side_B` to the trade dict at entry. The convention:

- `side_A`: `+1` long A when `direction=+1`, `−1` short A when `direction=−1`. Always `direction`.
- `side_B`: `+1` if `direction × sign(beta) < 0` (B is opposite of A when β>0); else flip when β<0. Concretely: `side_B = -direction × sign(beta)` for β≠0.
  - β>0, dir=+1 → A long, B short → side_B = −1 ✓
  - β>0, dir=−1 → A short, B long → side_B = +1 ✓
  - β<0, dir=+1 → A long, B long → side_B = +1 ✓ (matches `−1 × −1 = +1`)
  - β<0, dir=−1 → A short, B short → side_B = −1 ✓

# /antigravity-export — Export Antigravity Chat History

Export all Antigravity conversations to Markdown and JSON with full reasoning and timestamps, then place them into the current working directory.

Arguments passed: ``

---

## Steps

### 1. Check / install the tool

```bash
pip show antigravity-history
```

If not installed, run:

```bash
pip install antigravity-history
```

### 2. Rebuild indices (optional but recommended)

If the user passes `rebuild` as an argument, or if the export later produces no files, run:

```bash
aghistory rebuild
```

### 3. Export

Run from a temporary working directory so the output lands somewhere predictable:

```bash
cd "$TEMP" && aghistory export --full
```

The tool writes output to `$TEMP/antigravity_export/`.

If `aghistory` is not on PATH, fall back to:

```bash
python -m aghistory export --full
```

### 4. Check the report

Read `$TEMP/antigravity_export/export_report.txt` and note:
- How many conversations were exported
- How many (if any) were skipped and why

### 5. Merge all exports into one combined file

Create an `AI Chat History export/` folder in the current working directory. Then merge every `.md` file from the export into a single combined file.

Determine the week label from the current directory name (e.g. `Week 4` → `week4`). Name the output file `<weekLabel>_full_chat_history.md`.

Use this Python snippet to merge:

```python
import os, pathlib

export_dir = pathlib.Path(os.environ["TEMP"]) / "antigravity_export"
out_dir = pathlib.Path.cwd() / "AI Chat History export"
out_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# Derive week label from cwd
cwd_name = pathlib.Path.cwd().name.lower().replace(" ", "")  # e.g. "week4"
out_file = out_dir / f"{cwd_name}_full_chat_history.md"

md_files = sorted(export_dir.glob("*.md"))
with open(out_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    for i, f in enumerate(md_files):
        if i > 0:
            out.write("\n\n---\n\n")
        out.write(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

print(f"Merged {len(md_files)} files → {out_file}")
```

Run it with `python -c "<above code>"` or write it to a temp `.py` file and run it.

Tell the user:
- The output file path
- How many conversations were merged
- The total size of the combined file

---

## Argument dispatch

| Argument | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| *(none)* | Run the full export flow above |
| `rebuild` | Run `aghistory rebuild` first, then export |
| `rebuild-only` | Run `aghistory rebuild` and stop |
| `install` | Install / upgrade `antigravity-history` and confirm version |

---

## Notes

- History `.pb` files are in `%USERPROFILE%\.gemini\antigravity` on Windows.
- `--full` is always passed — this captures hidden AI reasoning and exact timestamps.
- Never delete or overwrite the source `.pb` files.
- If the export produces empty files, suggest running `aghistory rebuild` first.

# /antigravity-export — Export Full AI Chat History (Antigravity + Claude Code)

Exports **all** conversations for the current week — both from Antigravity and Claude Code — and merges them into a single combined Markdown file named `<weekN>_full_chat_history.md`.

Arguments passed: ``

---

## Step 1 — Detect current week

Inspect the current working directory (`cwd`) to extract the week label.

Examples:
- `D:/Quant Finance/Quant Program/Week 4` → `week4`
- `D:/Quant Finance/Quant Program/Week 0/Vibe Coding Task` → `week0`

Also record the **full week folder path** (e.g. `D:/Quant Finance/Quant Program/Week 4`). This is used to filter both Antigravity and Claude Code sessions.

---

## Step 2 — Export Antigravity history

Run:
```bash
aghistory export --full
```

If `aghistory` is not installed, run `pip install antigravity-history` first.

The output goes to `%TEMP%/antigravity_export/`. Each conversation is its own `.md` file. Each file contains a `**Workspace**` metadata field at the top that encodes the folder path, e.g.:

```
**Workspace**: file:///d:/Quant%20Finance/Quant%20Program/Week%204
```

---

## Step 3 — Filter Antigravity files by week

Write and run this Python script to filter only the sessions belonging to the current week:

```python
import pathlib, os, sys, urllib.parse, re

TEMP_EXPORT = pathlib.Path(os.environ["TEMP"]) / "antigravity_export"

# Derive week folder from cwd — walk up until we find a "Week N" segment
cwd = pathlib.Path.cwd()
week_folder = None
for part in cwd.parts:
    if re.match(r"(?i)^week\s*\d+$", part):
        # Reconstruct path up to and including this segment
        idx = cwd.parts.index(part)
        week_folder = pathlib.Path(*cwd.parts[:idx+1])
        break

if not week_folder:
    print("ERROR: Could not detect a Week N folder in the current path.")
    sys.exit(1)

# Normalise for matching inside Workspace URL
# e.g. "D:/Quant Finance/Quant Program/Week 4"
week_path_str = str(week_folder).replace("\\", "/")
week_encoded = urllib.parse.quote(week_path_str, safe="/:")

# Match either raw or URL-encoded form, case-insensitive
def matches_week(md_text):
    lower = md_text.lower()
    return (week_path_str.lower() in lower) or (week_encoded.lower() in lower)

md_files = sorted(TEMP_EXPORT.glob("*.md"))
matched = [f for f in md_files if matches_week(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore"))]

print(f"Week folder: {week_folder}")
print(f"Antigravity sessions found: {len(matched)} / {len(md_files)} total")
for f in matched:
    print(f"  - {f.name}")
```

Store `matched` for use in Step 5.

---

## Step 4 — Export Claude Code sessions for this week

Claude Code stores sessions as `.jsonl` files in:
`~/.claude/projects/<encoded-path>/`

The encoded path is the week folder path with non-alphanumeric chars replaced by `-` and lowercased.
Example: `D:/Quant Finance/Quant Program/Week 4` → `d--Quant-Finance-Quant-Program-Week-4`

Write and run this Python script to convert Claude Code sessions to Markdown:

```python
import pathlib, json, re
from datetime import datetime

CLAUDE_PROJECTS = pathlib.Path.home() / ".claude" / "projects"

# Find the matching project folder
cwd = pathlib.Path.cwd()
week_folder = None
for part in cwd.parts:
    if re.match(r"(?i)^week\s*\d+$", part):
        idx = cwd.parts.index(part)
        week_folder = pathlib.Path(*cwd.parts[:idx+1])
        break

def encode_project_path(p):
    """Match Claude Code's folder naming: replace non-alphanumeric with '-', lowercase drive letter."""
    s = str(p).replace("\\", "/")
    result = ""
    for ch in s:
        if ch.isalnum() or ch == "-":
            result += ch
        elif ch == "/":
            result += "-"
        else:
            result += "-"
    # Collapse multiple dashes
    result = re.sub(r"-+", "-", result).strip("-")
    return result

encoded = encode_project_path(week_folder)
# Try both exact and case variants
candidates = [
    CLAUDE_PROJECTS / encoded,
    CLAUDE_PROJECTS / encoded.lower(),
]
# Also search for any folder matching the week name
for folder in CLAUDE_PROJECTS.iterdir():
    week_part = week_folder.name.lower().replace(" ", "-")
    if week_part in folder.name.lower():
        candidates.append(folder)

project_dir = next((c for c in candidates if c.exists()), None)

if not project_dir:
    print(f"No Claude Code project folder found for {week_folder}")
    cc_sections = []
else:
    print(f"Claude Code project folder: {project_dir}")
    jsonl_files = sorted(project_dir.glob("*.jsonl"),
                         key=lambda f: f.stat().st_mtime)
    cc_sections = []

    for jf in jsonl_files:
        lines = jf.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore").strip().splitlines()
        if not lines:
            continue

        # Get session slug / title
        first = json.loads(lines[0])
        slug = first.get("slug") or jf.stem[:8]
        start_ts = first.get("timestamp", "")[:10]

        messages = []
        for raw in lines:
            try:
                entry = json.loads(raw)
            except Exception:
                continue

            role = None
            content_text = ""

            if entry.get("type") == "user":
                role = "User"
                msg = entry.get("message", {})
                content = msg.get("content", "")
                if isinstance(content, str):
                    content_text = content
                elif isinstance(content, list):
                    parts = []
                    for c in content:
                        if isinstance(c, dict):
                            if c.get("type") == "text":
                                parts.append(c.get("text", ""))
                            elif c.get("type") == "tool_result":
                                inner = c.get("content", "")
                                if isinstance(inner, list):
                                    for i in inner:
                                        if isinstance(i, dict) and i.get("type") == "text":
                                            parts.append(f"[Tool Result]: {i.get('text','')[:300]}")
                                elif isinstance(inner, str):
                                    parts.append(f"[Tool Result]: {inner[:300]}")
                    content_text = "\n".join(parts)

            elif entry.get("type") == "assistant":
                role = "Assistant"
                msg = entry.get("message", {})
                content = msg.get("content", "")
                if isinstance(content, str):
                    content_text = content
                elif isinstance(content, list):
                    parts = []
                    for c in content:
                        if isinstance(c, dict):
                            if c.get("type") == "text":
                                parts.append(c.get("text", ""))
                            elif c.get("type") == "tool_use":
                                tool_name = c.get("name", "unknown")
                                tool_input = json.dumps(c.get("input", {}), indent=2)[:500]
                                parts.append(f"[Tool Call: {tool_name}]\n```json\n{tool_input}\n```")
                    content_text = "\n".join(parts)

            if role and content_text.strip():
                ts = entry.get("timestamp", "")[:19].replace("T", " ")
                messages.append((role, ts, content_text.strip()))

        if messages:
            header = f"## Claude Code Session: {slug}\n**Date**: {start_ts}  |  **Messages**: {len(messages)}\n"
            body = "\n\n".join(
                f"### {role} `{ts}`\n{text}" for role, ts, text in messages
            )
            cc_sections.append(header + "\n" + body)
            print(f"  Session {jf.name}: {len(messages)} messages")

print(f"\nClaude Code sections to merge: {len(cc_sections)}")
```

Store `cc_sections` (list of Markdown strings) for Step 5.

## Step 5 — Merge into one combined file

Write and run this Python script that combines both sources:

```python
import pathlib, os, re, urllib.parse
from datetime import datetime

# --- re-run detection ---
cwd = pathlib.Path.cwd()
week_folder = None
for part in cwd.parts:
    if re.match(r"(?i)^week\s*\d+$", part):
        idx = cwd.parts.index(part)
        week_folder = pathlib.Path(*cwd.parts[:idx+1])
        break

week_label = week_folder.name.lower().replace(" ", "")  # e.g. "week4"

out_dir = week_folder / "AI Chat History export"
out_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
out_file = out_dir / f"{week_label}_full_chat_history.md"

TEMP_EXPORT = pathlib.Path(os.environ["TEMP"]) / "antigravity_export"
week_path_str = str(week_folder).replace("\\", "/")
week_encoded = urllib.parse.quote(week_path_str, safe="/:")

def matches_week(text):
    lower = text.lower()
    return (week_path_str.lower() in lower) or (week_encoded.lower() in lower)

ag_files = sorted(TEMP_EXPORT.glob("*.md"))
ag_matched = [f for f in ag_files if matches_week(f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore"))]

sections = []

# --- Antigravity section ---
if ag_matched:
    ag_parts = []
    for f in ag_matched:
        ag_parts.append(f"### {f.stem}\n\n" + f.read_text(encoding="utf-8", errors="ignore"))
    sections.append("# Antigravity Chat History\n\n" + "\n\n---\n\n".join(ag_parts))

# --- Claude Code section ---
# (cc_sections is injected from Step 4 — paste that script output here or re-run inline)
# If running as a single merged script, include cc_sections directly.

with open(out_file, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    out.write(f"# AI Chat History — {week_folder.name}\n")
    out.write(f"*Exported: {datetime.utcnow().strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M UTC')}*\n\n")
    out.write("---\n\n")
    out.write("\n\n---\n\n".join(sections))

print(f"\nOutput: {out_file}")
print(f"Size:   {out_file.stat().st_size / 1024:.1f} KB")
```
